intro: This page maps common public claims to what Illustrative Manuscripts actually contains — open CNTR transcriptions, a bounded 1–400 CE Greek NT slice, and hand-curated Qurʾān catalog data. It is meant to help students, researchers, debaters, and apologists stay precise: neither inflating our counts nor pretending the site settles every tradition-scale debate.

pathways.title: Student
pathways.description: Learn how to read a witness card, what our numbers mean, and where block-level famous passages differ from the word census.

pathways.title: Researcher / academic
pathways.description: Download the open census, read methodology, and cite CNTR/INTF for primaries — cite us for the illustrative collation slice only.

pathways.title: Debater / apologist
pathways.description: Check claim discipline before arguing from our charts — then use Famous passages, Variants, Uthmanic rasm, and Coverage honesty together.

claims.claim: Nobody has counted New Testament variants.
claims.why: Peter Gurry (NTS 2016) estimates on the order of ~500,000 readings across the whole Greek tradition — a extrapolation, not a hand count of every manuscript. Our site does publish a mechanical count, but only for word-aligned disagreements vs SR GNT in extant letters of our 1–400 CE CNTR witness slice — not the full ~5,700+ manuscript tradition.

scholarship.label: Gurry 2016 — How Many Variants Are in the Greek New Testament?

claims.claim: The New Testament text is completely unknown before late manuscripts.
claims.why: Within our frozen window, substantial Greek material survives from the second and third centuries (papyri) plus fourth-century codices such as 01 and 03. That does not recover every verse in every book from every century — but it falsifies the blanket claim that nothing early exists.

claims.claim: By about 400 CE the Greek New Testament text is largely recoverable.
claims.why: Standard critical-edition framing (and our site’s own scope statement) treats the fourth-century major codices plus earlier papyri as the backbone for reconstructing the Greek text — while still not counting every later Byzantine variant or replacing NA28/ECM apparatus judgments.

claims.claim: P66, P75, 01, and 03 lack the Pericope Adulterae (John 7:53–8:11).
claims.why: In CNTR transcriptions in our corpus, that block is marked absent; narrative runs from 7:52 to 8:12 in those witnesses. Later Byzantine copies insert the pericope — a different story from our early slice.

claims.claim: Mark originally ended at 16:8 in the earliest complete Greek codices in our window.
claims.why: Codex Sinaiticus (01) and Codex Vaticanus (03) end Mark at 16:8 in the main Greek tradition represented in CNTR; the longer ending 16:9–20 is a later supplement in the manuscript record. Textual critics still debate composition history — our data support the codex-level statement for 01/03.

claims.claim: The Comma Johanneum is in the earliest Greek tradition.
claims.why: 1 John 5:7–8 is extant in early Greek witnesses with the short reading (Spirit, water, blood). The explicit heavenly Trinity wording of the Comma is not attested in Greek before the sixteenth century; it entered some Latin lines and late Greek retro-translations.

claims.claim: The Lord’s Prayer doxology (“For thine is the kingdom…”) is in the earliest Alexandrian Greek witnesses of Matthew.
claims.why: In CNTR transcriptions for Codex Sinaiticus (01) and Codex Vaticanus (03), Matthew 6:13 is extant but the Greek ends at the petition against evil — the closing doxology familiar from the KJV is not part of that early line. Later Byzantine copies and liturgical tradition supplied the formula; NA28/UBS5 omit it from Matthew.

claims.claim: Acts 8:37 (the Ethiopian’s confession before baptism) is in our earliest Greek witnesses of Acts.
claims.why: CNTR marks Acts 8:37 absent (—) in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and 𝔓⁴⁵ within our 1–400 CE slice; the narrative runs from 8:36 to 8:38. The verse is common in Byzantine copies and the Textus Receptus — a later expansion, not the earliest recoverable Greek in our window.

claims.claim: Mark 9:44 and 9:46 (duplicate “unquenchable fire” warnings) are in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.
claims.why: In CNTR, both verses are marked absent (—) in 01 and 03; the saying appears once at Mark 9:48 in that line. Duplicated lines persist in the Byzantine majority and KJV — scribal assimilation to a longer form, not the earliest complete Greek codices in our dataset.

claims.claim: The Qurʾān has no manuscript variation.
claims.why: The Uthmanic Text Type is highly uniform, but published stemmatics (Cook; Sidky; van Putten) report on the order of ~35–40 regional rasm differences among the four ʿUthmānic exemplar traditions — not wholesale content rewrites, but not zero graphic variation. Early palimpsests such as Ṣanʿāʾ 1 preserve a lower text that is not UT.

scholarship.label: Cook — The Koran: A Very Short Introduction (regional rasm overview)

claims.claim: From about 650 CE the Uthmanic text type is already stable.
claims.why: Sidky and van Putten’s archetype framing treats UT as stable from the seventh century onward for the rasm tradition they model — while allowing later scribal noise and regional graphic differences, not a claim of byte-identical copies everywhere.

claims.claim: Early Qurʾān manuscripts show random independent spelling at each niʿmat allāh verse.
claims.why: Van Putten (BSOAS 2019) collated fourteen early witnesses plus the Cairo reference for niʿmat allāh / rabbi-ka: at nearly every attested verse they share the same ta vs ta marbūṭa choice as the 1924 rasm — including grammatically quirky pairings — with only isolated disagreements (e.g. Q 16:114, Q 37:57). That pattern fits a shared written archetype copied from exemplars, not independent invention at each verse.

scholarship.label: van Putten 2019 — The Grace of God (open access)

claims.claim: Shared idiosyncratic spellings in early Uthmanic manuscripts support a written Uthmanic archetype.
claims.why: Within scope of published collation work (van Putten 2019; stemma framing in Cook and Sidky): when many early UT manuscripts agree on the same non-standard rasm at the same ayah — the niʿmat case is the site’s illustrative proof — the straightforward scholarly explanation is descent from a single written archetype and copying from written exemplars. That is early standardization of a text type, not a claim about zero variation (see regional rasm) or about proving ʿUthmān’s personal authorship.

claims.claim: Illustrative Manuscripts proves intentional theological corruption at scale.
claims.why: Optional intentional-vs-error tags on some Greek NT units are heuristic and model-assisted — useful for exploration, not proof of motive across the tradition. Most counted units are spelling, word order, or ordinary scribal difference vs SR GNT.

links.label: Cite & learn — what we are not claiming

claims.claim: Our census equals the NA28 apparatus or all Greek manuscripts.
claims.why: Out of scope by design: we mechanically align a bounded CNTR witness set to SR GNT. NA28/ECM/IGNTP record editorial judgments and thousands of witnesses beyond our 1–400 CE illustrative slice.

claims.claim: The Masoretic Text is identical to what Jesus read.
claims.why: Second-Temple and pre-Christian Hebrew witnesses in our corpus (Dead Sea Scrolls, Nash Papyrus) show a largely continuous consonantal tradition alongside spelling diversity and occasional longer or shorter readings in some books. That supports substantial continuity for much of the Hebrew Bible — not byte-identical identity with every medieval Masoretic codex for every verse a first-century reader might have heard.

scholarship.label: Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (3rd ed.) — DSS vs MT overview

claims.claim: The Septuagint is a late Christian invention.
claims.why: Jewish Greek Torah and prophetic books are attested on pre-Christian papyri in this site’s Hebrew/LXX slice — e.g. P.Ryl. 458 (Genesis), P.Fouad 266 (Deuteronomy), P.Oxy. 1007 (Exodus) — centuries before Christian recensions and church fathers. Later Christian copies and revisions exist; that is not the same as inventing the whole Greek Old Testament tradition.

scholarship.label: Rahlfs / Göttingen LXX — pre-Christian Jewish Greek witnesses

claims.claim: 1QIsaᵃ proves the Bible never changed.
claims.why: The Great Isaiah Scroll agrees with the Masoretic book of Isaiah far more often than it disagrees — a key data point for stability. It also preserves thousands of spelling variants and documented textual differences elsewhere in the DSS corpus; “remarkable agreement in Isaiah” is not a license to claim zero textual history for the whole Hebrew Bible.

scholarship.label: Ulrich, The Biblical Qumran Scrolls (DJD series) — 1QIsaᵃ edition

claims.claim: The Old Testament survives only in medieval manuscripts — nothing earlier exists.
claims.why: Within our Hebrew/LXX window, material survives from the second century BCE onward (DSS) and from pre-Christian Greek papyri. That does not recover every book on every leaf for every century — but it falsifies the blanket claim that no pre-medieval witnesses exist.

claims.claim: Nag Hammadi texts are lost books of the New Testament canon.
claims.why: The find shows how diverse early Christian literature was — and some titles (e.g. Gospel of Thomas) overlap sayings also known from Greek fragments. But these are fourth-century Coptic codices of mostly Gnostic tractates, not uncatalogued Greek NT manuscript copies. Church lists debated individual works; they were not treated as the same stream as Matthew–Revelation in the Greek NT tradition this site collates (1–400 CE CNTR).

scholarship.label: Ehrman, Lost Christianities — canon formation vs diversity
